analysis: Brokskat boo father and saeno boo father's brother contain an expressive kinship base. Bāppa/buba and regional paternal terms compete; a precise old source cannot be selected from boo alone. The uncle phrase has modifier plus father, so it is not an unextended kinship reflex.
SchmidtKaul2008p247 explicitly identifies Brokskat sokpaa feather and nyaa fish as Purik loans; their stress belongs to loan adaptation rather than inherited pakṣa or matsya change.

Ushojo baṛo moṣ feces is a big-plus-excretion expression paired with child/small moṣ urine. Its modifier and possible urinary noun must be split before etymology or accent; it is not a direct gūtha reflex.

Printed SchmidtKaulp275item209 has two Brokskat alternatives, 'apo and k'ii. The DB kiii 'apo string reverses or concatenates them and introduces apparent triple i. The apo branch belongs to álpa722; k'ii needs an independent quantity-interrogative or small-word derivation. Use lexical splits, not whole-record inheritance.

Brokskat bun field is a candidate counterpart to Gilgit baan cultivated field and vāpana11523, but nasal and vowel history and potential local borrowing remain to be established. It is not a kṣētra reflex merely by field gloss.

SchmidtKaul2008p248 explicitly labels Brokskat kheey field a loan from an unidentified Indo-Aryan language. Khēṭa and kṣētra are competing ultimate inputs; no inherited Brokskat accent prediction is assigned.

Ushojo dege du bi fifty and du bi forty, and Brokskat dobuẓu ek forty-one, are renewed numerical compounds involving ten/two/twenty/one. Their multiword stress and morphology must be analyzed compositionally; they are not simple descendants of an old decimal numeral.

Brokskat anjiir fig is the regional anjīr-type fruit name, not phalgu. A Persian ultimate source is well motivated by form and referent, with the immediate Kashmiri/Urdu route still open; no inherited phalgu accent exception is counted.

Ushojo rabaṛ fight has repeated rhotic/retroflex material but no secure match to vigraha or milati. An expressive action noun or contact term remains possible; first stress is retained without a forced link.
Brokskat šoor fire may invite comparison with śuc/śoka or a regional fire term, but neither root correspondence is secure here. Its old ancestry and modern tone remain unassigned.

Ushojo awwal first and jinaazo funeral bier match regional Arabic-origin awwal/janāza vocabulary. The immediate Urdu/Pashto/Hindko route is not established; they are contact-word stress observations rather than inherited Sanskrit cases.
Ushojo jaṇḍ flea does not support a direct pluṣi derivation. An expressive or regional insect name needs independent identification.
Ushojo kaṣar flood has final stress but is not a convincing avaḍḍhāla cognate. A torrent/breaking or regional watercourse noun remains to be investigated.
Brokskat iuthis fly is a verb in the action list, not the fly insect. Ud-/uḍḍ flight roots are candidates, but the th and citation is material must be identified before linking.

Brokskat kuti foot could reflect a knee/leg term related to kuṭ/kuṭṭa rather than pāda; first stress does not justify a semantically convenient pāda link. Compare lower-limb terminology and local polysemy.

SchmidtKaul2008p247 identifies dzaygal forest as a Kashmiri-mediated regional jungle loan. Tshoq is a separate forest word with no established Indo-Aryan ancestry here; it is not automatically jhalla bush.

Raw Ushojo supplement prints fortnight; half a moon horomos with the English continuation on the next line. The DB placed a moon after the phonetic word. Horomos plausibly contains half plus month; exact components and accent must be checked separately.
Ushojo sindaxa frog is not a segmental match to maṇḍūka. A regional expressive animal name is possible, but no old accent reconstruction is assigned.

The Brokskat record combines peree and punjis full, which may continue different pūr- formations. The primary table must determine their exact ordering and accent; one whole-record family assignment would conflate these alternatives.

Ushojo lišim garlic is a candidate láśuna10990 derivative or regional continuation, preferable semantically and segmentally to the retrieved uṣṇa onion. Full Turner10990 supplies many lasun/lasūṇ variants but no direct lišim; final n-to-m and first-vowel fronting remain unexplained, so the proposal is explicitly provisional.
Ushojo gaṭono get in the future may reflect a get/obtain derivative with a future suffix, but gr̥bhāyati alone does not explain ṭ. Recover the verbal paradigm before accepting a cognate link.

Brokskat dis give and dis day occupy different source rows and have separate immediate histories, dā/give versus divasa/day. The DB merges them by spelling. They require sense-specific branches, not a single family assignment.

Brokskat chaati/chal female goat plausibly belongs to chagala, but the exact t/l and derivative relation needs source confirmation. Male miar and ẓatoo are distinct names, potentially caprid species or expressive/contact terms; no common ancestry is inferred from goat gloss alone.

Ushojo liolo zar gold is a yellow/red-color modifier plus the regional zar gold word. The whole phrase is not an inherited suvarṇa reflex; the color component and contact metal term must be analyzed separately.
Brokskat thaalo good has no secure segmental match to śubha or mr̥ṣṭa. A local evaluative adjective or loan needs evidence; first stress is recorded but not used to invent ancestry.

Brokskat pyyei granddaughter may belong to pautrī and the putr/pautr kinship network, but the missing affricate and vowel sequence require a specific feminine derivation. Retain as a candidate rather than a strict cognate.

Brokskat min grease plausibly matches mḗdas, while sunny side of mountain could be a separate homonym or semantic development. The source rows66/105 must be distinguished before assigning the entire merged record to fat ancestry.
